lessons.title: Nuclear fission and fusion
lessons.summary: Compare nuclear fission and nuclear fusion, describe how a chain reaction is controlled in a reactor, and explain why fusion powers the stars but is so hard to achieve on Earth.
objectives: I can describe what happens during nuclear fission of a large unstable nucleus such as uranium-235.
I can explain how a chain reaction occurs and how it is controlled in a nuclear reactor.
I can describe nuclear fusion and explain why it needs very high temperatures and pressures.
I can compare fission and fusion in terms of the nuclei involved and the energy released.
I can describe the products of fission and the risks associated with them.

activities.title: Nuclear fission
activities.content:
## Splitting a large nucleus

**Nuclear fission** is the splitting of a **large, unstable nucleus** into two smaller nuclei. The nuclei used in reactors are usually **uranium-235** or **plutonium-239**.

Spontaneous fission (a nucleus splitting on its own) is very rare. In practice, fission is **induced**: the large nucleus **absorbs a neutron**, becomes even more unstable, and then splits.

When a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes fission it produces:
- **Two smaller nuclei** (called daughter nuclei or fission products), which are roughly the same size as each other. These are **radioactive**.
- **Two or three neutrons**.
- **Gamma radiation**.

```
  n  +  U-235  →  U-236 (unstable)  →  Ba-141  +  Kr-92  +  3n  +  energy
```

The products carry a huge amount of **kinetic energy**. The total mass of the products is very slightly less than the mass of the original nucleus plus neutron; that tiny missing mass has been released as energy. Per atom, fission releases millions of times more energy than a chemical reaction such as burning.

All of the energy released ends up in the kinetic energy of the fragments and the gamma rays, and in a reactor this is used to heat water into steam that drives turbines and generators.

question.text: Which THREE of the following are produced when a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes fission after absorbing a neutron?
question.hint: Think about what is left after a big nucleus splits, and what is emitted along with the fragments.
question.explanation: Fission produces two smaller daughter nuclei, two or three neutrons and gamma radiation. Alpha particles are not produced by fission, and the nucleus does not remain uranium-235.

options.feedback: Alpha emission is a form of radioactive decay, not fission.

activities.title: Chain reactions
activities.content:
## One fission leads to another

Each fission releases **two or three neutrons**. If those neutrons are absorbed by **other** uranium-235 nuclei, they cause **more fissions**, which release more neutrons, and so on. This is a **chain reaction**.

```
            → fission → 3n → ...
 n → fission → fission → 3n → ...
            → fission → 3n → ...
```

If every fission causes more than one further fission, the number of fissions grows rapidly. In a **nuclear weapon** the chain reaction is deliberately **uncontrolled**, releasing enormous energy in a fraction of a second.

In a **nuclear reactor** the chain reaction is **controlled** so that, on average, exactly **one** neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission. The reaction then runs steadily, releasing energy at a constant rate.

**Parts of a reactor**
- **Fuel rods**: contain uranium-235.
- **Moderator** (often graphite or water): **slows down** the neutrons, because slow neutrons are much more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 and cause fission.
- **Control rods** (boron or cadmium): **absorb neutrons**. Lowering the rods into the core absorbs more neutrons and slows the reaction; raising them speeds it up. Fully inserting them shuts the reactor down.
- **Coolant**: carries the thermal energy away to make steam.
- **Concrete and steel shielding**: absorbs radiation to protect workers.

activities.title: Worked example: reasoning about a reactor
activities.content:
**A reactor operator notices the power output is rising too quickly. Explain what should be done and why it works.**

1. Rising power means more than one neutron from each fission is going on to cause further fissions.
2. The operator should **lower the control rods** further into the core.
3. The control rods are made of a material such as boron that **absorbs neutrons**.
4. Fewer neutrons are available to be absorbed by uranium nuclei, so **fewer fissions** occur per second.
5. The chain reaction slows until each fission causes, on average, exactly one more, and the power output becomes steady again.

**Counting neutrons.** Suppose each fission releases 3 neutrons and the process starts with one fission. If there were no control and every neutron caused a fission:

| Generation | Fissions |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 3 |
| 3 | 9 |
| 4 | 27 |
| 10 | 19 683 |

This exponential growth is why uncontrolled chain reactions are so violent.

question.text: In an uncontrolled chain reaction, each fission releases 2 neutrons and every neutron causes another fission. Starting from a single fission, how many fissions occur in the 6th generation?
question.explanation: Generation 1: 1, then 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The 6th generation has 2⁵ = 32 fissions.

question.text: Match each part of a nuclear reactor to its job.
question.hint: One slows neutrons, one absorbs them, one carries heat away.
question.explanation: The moderator slows neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission. Control rods absorb neutrons to control the rate. The coolant transfers the thermal energy out of the core.

pairs.right: Slows down the neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission
Absorb neutrons to control the rate of the chain reaction
Carries thermal energy away from the core to make steam

activities.title: Nuclear fusion
activities.content:
## Joining small nuclei

**Nuclear fusion** is the **joining of two light nuclei** to form a single heavier nucleus. The most common example is hydrogen nuclei fusing to form helium.

```
  H-2  +  H-3  →  He-4  +  n  +  energy
```

When the nuclei fuse, some of their mass is converted into energy, released mostly as **radiation** (gamma rays) and as the kinetic energy of the products. Kilogram for kilogram, fusion releases even **more** energy than fission.

**Why fusion is so difficult**

Nuclei are positively charged, so they **repel** each other strongly (electrostatic repulsion). To fuse, they must get close enough for the strong nuclear force to take over. That needs:
- **Extremely high temperatures** (millions of degrees) so the nuclei are moving fast enough to overcome the repulsion.
- **Very high pressures** so the nuclei are packed close together and collide often.

**Fusion in stars**: the enormous gravity of a star squeezes its core and heats it to around 15 million °C, so hydrogen fuses to helium continuously. This is the energy source of the Sun and every other star.

**Fusion on Earth**: experimental reactors use powerful magnetic fields to hold a super-hot plasma away from the walls. So far they use more energy to run than they produce, but the potential prize is enormous: the fuel (hydrogen isotopes) is plentiful and the waste is far less radioactive than from fission.

question.text: Why does nuclear fusion require extremely high temperatures?
question.hint: Both nuclei carry the same sign of charge.
question.explanation: Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. At very high temperatures they move fast enough to overcome this repulsion and get close enough to fuse.

options.text: So the nuclei move fast enough to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between them
So the nuclei melt into each other
So the electrons are removed and the nuclei become neutral
options.feedback: Removing electrons makes the nuclei more exposed, but they still repel.

options.text: Because heat is a product of fusion

activities.title: Comparing fission and fusion
activities.content:
## Side by side

| | Fission | Fusion |
|---|---|---|
| **What happens** | Large nucleus splits into two smaller ones | Two small nuclei join to form a larger one |
| **Typical nuclei** | Uranium-235, plutonium-239 | Hydrogen isotopes (deuterium, tritium) |
| **How it starts** | Nucleus absorbs a neutron | Nuclei collide at very high speed |
| **Conditions** | Works at ordinary temperatures with a moderator | Millions of degrees, very high pressure |
| **Energy per kg of fuel** | Very large | Even larger |
| **Where it happens** | Nuclear power stations, weapons | Stars, experimental reactors |
| **Main waste problem** | Highly radioactive daughter nuclei with long half-lives | Very little long-lived waste |

**Common mistakes to avoid**
- Fission is **not** radioactive decay. Decay happens spontaneously to a single nucleus; fission is usually triggered by a neutron and produces two large fragments.
- The **energy** in both cases comes from a small loss of mass, not from chemical bonds.
- Fusion does **not** happen in today's power stations; they all use fission.

**Storing fission waste**: the daughter nuclei are radioactive with a range of half-lives, some lasting thousands of years, so used fuel must be stored safely, deep underground, for a very long time.

question.text: True or false: the nuclear power stations that supply electricity to the UK use nuclear fusion.
question.hint: Which process can we currently sustain and control on Earth?
question.explanation: False. All current nuclear power stations use fission of uranium or plutonium. Fusion power is still experimental.

metadata.blanksText: In fission, a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a ___ and splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing two or three more of these particles and ___ radiation. In fusion, two ___ nuclei join together.

question.hint: The particle has no charge. The radiation is the most penetrating type. Fusion involves small nuclei.
question.explanation: A neutron is absorbed; gamma radiation is released; fusion joins light (small) nuclei such as hydrogen.

question.text:
Nuclear power stations use fission to generate electricity.

(a) Describe how a chain reaction is produced in the fuel of a nuclear reactor. (3 marks)

(b) Explain how control rods are used to keep the chain reaction at a steady rate. (2 marks)

(c) State one reason why the waste from a fission reactor is difficult to deal with. (1 mark)
question.hint: Neutron in, fission, neutrons out, those neutrons cause more fissions. Control rods absorb neutrons.
question.explanation: (a) A uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits, releasing two or three neutrons. These neutrons are absorbed by other uranium nuclei, causing them to split and release more neutrons, so the process keeps going. (b) Control rods absorb neutrons. Lowering them absorbs more neutrons so fewer fissions occur; raising them allows more fissions. They are adjusted so exactly one neutron per fission causes another fission. (c) The daughter nuclei are highly radioactive and some have very long half-lives, so the waste must be stored safely for thousands of years.

markScheme.criterion: A uranium nucleus absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission / splits
Two or three neutrons are released by each fission
These neutrons go on to cause further fissions so the process repeats
Rods are lowered / raised to change the number of neutrons available so that one fission leads to one more
Waste is highly radioactive / has long half-lives / must be stored for a very long time

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Fission**: a large unstable nucleus (U-235, Pu-239) absorbs a **neutron** and splits into two smaller radioactive nuclei + 2 or 3 neutrons + gamma rays + lots of kinetic energy.
- **Chain reaction**: the released neutrons cause more fissions. Uncontrolled in a bomb; **controlled** in a reactor so one fission leads to one more.
- **Moderator** slows neutrons; **control rods** absorb them; the coolant carries the energy away.
- **Fusion**: two **light** nuclei (hydrogen) join to make a heavier one, releasing even more energy per kg. Needs millions of degrees and huge pressure to overcome electrostatic repulsion. Powers stars.
- Fission waste is highly radioactive with long half-lives; fusion produces far less long-lived waste.

practiceQuestions.text: Which isotope is commonly used as fuel in fission reactors?
practiceQuestions.hint: It is a very heavy element.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Uranium-235 is the usual fuel; plutonium-239 is also used. Hydrogen and helium are involved in fusion, not fission.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: nuclear fusion is the process that releases energy in the Sun.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. In the Sun's core hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing energy.

practiceQuestions.text: What is the job of the moderator in a nuclear reactor?
practiceQuestions.hint: Fast neutrons tend to fly straight past uranium nuclei.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The moderator slows the neutrons down so they are much more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 nuclei and cause fission.

options.text: To slow down neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission
To absorb neutrons and stop the reaction
options.feedback: That is the job of the control rods.

options.text: To carry thermal energy out of the core

practiceQuestions.text: Put these steps of a fission chain reaction in order.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start with a neutron approaching a nucleus.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A neutron is absorbed, the nucleus becomes unstable and splits, neutrons and energy are released, and those neutrons are absorbed by other nuclei.
order: A slow neutron is absorbed by a uranium-235 nucleus
The nucleus becomes unstable and splits into two smaller nuclei
Two or three neutrons and gamma radiation are released
The released neutrons are absorbed by other uranium-235 nuclei

practiceQuestions.text: A uranium-235 nucleus (92 protons, 143 neutrons) absorbs one neutron and splits into a barium-141 nucleus, a krypton-92 nucleus and some free neutrons. Use mass numbers to work out how many free neutrons are released.
practiceQuestions.hint: Total mass number before = 235 + 1. Total after = 141 + 92 + number of neutrons.

practiceQuestions.text: Two hydrogen nuclei, deuterium (mass number 2) and tritium (mass number 3), fuse to form a helium nucleus of mass number 4. What is the mass number of the other particle released?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 2 + 3 = 5, and 5 − 4 = 1. The extra particle is a single neutron with mass number 1.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each statement to fission or fusion.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fusion joins light nuclei and happens in stars. Fission splits a heavy nucleus after neutron absorption.

pairs.left: A heavy nucleus splits after absorbing a neutron
Two light nuclei join to form a heavier one

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO conditions are needed for nuclear fusion to take place?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what it takes to force two positive nuclei together.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fusion needs very high temperatures so the nuclei move fast enough to overcome repulsion, and very high pressures so they are close together and collide often.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why nuclear fusion is very difficult to achieve in a reactor on Earth.
practiceQuestions.hint: What force acts between two positive nuclei, and what is needed to overcome it?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so extremely high temperatures and pressures are needed to bring them close enough to fuse. Producing and containing such conditions takes enormous amounts of energy and very advanced technology.

markScheme.criterion: Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other
Very high temperature and/or pressure needed, which is hard to produce or contain

practiceQuestions.text:
A newspaper article claims that fusion power stations would be safer than fission power stations.

(a) Give one difference between the nuclear reactions used in fission and fusion. (1 mark)

(b) Explain one reason why fusion could produce less dangerous waste than fission. (2 marks)

(c) Suggest one reason why fusion power stations are not yet in use. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare what happens to the nuclei, what the products are, and how hard the conditions are to achieve.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Fission splits a large nucleus into two smaller ones; fusion joins two small nuclei. (b) Fission produces daughter nuclei that are highly radioactive with long half-lives, whereas the main product of fusion is helium, which is not radioactive, so far less long-lived waste is produced. (c) The very high temperatures and pressures are extremely difficult to create and contain, and current experiments use more energy than they produce.

markScheme.criterion: Fission splits a large nucleus; fusion joins small nuclei
Fission products are highly radioactive / have long half-lives
Fusion product (helium) is not radioactive / much less long-lived waste
The extreme temperature / pressure is hard to achieve or contain, or the process uses more energy than it produces
